title: Pudding and the Moonpetal Berries
markdown:
In the Archipelago of Whispering Peaks, cliffs dropped into misty chasms and ropes thick as dragon tails stretched between summits like a spider’s web. Meadows of cloud were a feast for sheep with wool like spun moonlight. Deep caves sometimes held a glint of treasure.

Pudding was an ogre of very large size and even more gentle. His tummy rumbled with quiet thoughts, not roaring intentions. He loved a warm mug of dandelion tea, brewed just right, and a cozy window where sunbeams painted distant peaks gold and rose. His constant companion was Button, a hen the colour of polished buttons, sharp bright eyes that missed nothing, a splash of cheerful energy in his calm world.

This morning, first pale rays stretching like sleepy cats across a mossy roof, Pudding’s big chest felt a familiar lurch. Shoulders sagged. The dread of being volunteered. The good folk of the Whispering Peaks were lovely, with a funny habit: they spotted the biggest, neatest-looking creature and assumed that creature was best for every daring, dramatic, noisy task. Pudding, by nature, was the biggest and, in his quiet way, the neatest. His order was the sleeping-forest kind.

He stirred tea with a spoon carved from fallen birch. “I’ve only just woken, and already I feel the weight of expectation. I haven’t even had my second biscuit, and the world seems to be planning my heroic deeds.” A sigh like wind in dry leaves.

The wish for a biscuit-filled day dashed quicker than a dewdrop from a web. Iridescent wings, a thousand tiny rainbows: the Flutterwings, tiny shimmering folk from a glittering peak. Their leader Pip, particularly bright, hovered at the door, little face etched with what she believed was great concern.

“Pudding, dear fellow!” Silver bells. “A most urgent, most delightful problem! A patch of Moonpetal Cloud-Berries has bloomed on the Sunken Spire, needed for the Grand Midsummer Festival! Your strength, your grandness, is precisely what is required. No one else is quite so imposing!”

Pudding blinked. The Sunken Spire: crumbling paths, sudden sheer drops. Retrieving berries sounded remarkably like volunteering for something dramatic. “Perhaps someone smaller? Who can flutter more easily? Less likely to disturb the peaceful feeling of the Spire?”

“Nonsense!” Pip tugged his sleeve with surprising strength. “Your plan will be the most sensible! We’ve already drawn it out!” A scroll of perfectly drawn tiny arrows and neat boxes, Flutterwing precision. “Ascend the Giant’s Staircase, cross the Gossamer Bridge, voilà! Berries!”

Neat. Also, he suspected, about as clever as a pebble trying to fly. The Staircase was famous for loose stones tumbling with alarming regularity. The Gossamer Bridge was named for a reason: solidified moonlight, substantial as a whisper. Flutterwing eyes gleamed with the certainty of their perfectly planned adventure, more unnerving than a rogue gust.

Button hopped onto the table and pecked the scroll, once, as if testing whether paper could be reasoned with. It could not.

“We cannot possibly panic yet,” Pudding said to Button on his shoulder, tiny claws in thick fur. “We have not even had tea. This plan requires further thought. Careful, quiet thought.” Button clucked wisely, head bobbing.

Against better judgment, to avoid a long debate that would lead to more volunteering and more diagrams, he agreed. He packed a flask of leftover tea, because journeys without tea were a kind of noise. They set off, Button pecking his ear with encouraging clucks, following the meticulously drawn map.

The Giant’s Staircase wobbled like jelly on a plate in an earthquake. Pudding placed each enormous foot with a clockmaker’s care. A stone clattered away into mist; he waited until the clatter finished before he trusted the next step. Button scurried ahead, small claws finding purchase, a tiny beacon of agility against his deliberate might.

Pip hovered, drawing a new arrow in the air with one finger. “Faster is neater!” Pudding did not go faster. The mountain, he felt, preferred manners.

Pip’s neat plan led them to the Gossamer Bridge, shimmering, thin as a spider’s thread of moonlight. “Right then,” she trilled from a safe distance. “Pudding, step gingerly. Button can watch from here. Wouldn’t want feathers ruffled.”

A cautious step. The bridge swayed, a dizzying dance. Groan of snapping fibres, chill mist from the chasm, sheer drop. Another tentative step; a sigh of tired silk; a section ahead snapped. Stuck, suspended over mist. Flutterwings in distress, neat plan unravelled.

Wind tugging sturdy trousers, mist like curious ghosts: Pudding’s quiet cleverness bloomed. The Flutterwings, in their desire for order and perfectly drawn lines, had overlooked sturdy reality. “Neatest,” he mumbled at the broken bridge, “does not always mean cleverest. Sometimes it just means neat.”

He looked at Button. Button looked back, button-eyes sparkling with more than hen-sense. Partner, not pet. Deep breath: damp earth, distant pine. Below the broken bridge, a cluster of sturdy mountain flowers, roots clinging like brave little soldiers.

A gust smelling of ozone and lavender. Wizard Basil appeared, beard tangled with more spell components than a shop, robes patched with what looked like discarded tapestry, gnarled staff pulsing soft blue. “Ah, Pudding! A predicament! My patented Bridge-Binder charm would have secured that beautifully! Sprinkle the enchanted dust precisely along the weak points!” A small shimmering pouch.

Elegant, precise magical theory. Pudding saw another problem Basil’s wizardly eyes, focused on enchantment, had missed. The pouch was tiny; the bridge, even broken, was long. How to sprinkle precisely without falling, or wasting precious dust?

He counted the snapped strands. There were more of them than there was dust. Arithmetic, in Pudding’s experience, was a kind of kindness.

“Thank you, Wizard Basil.” Still scanning. A narrow dark opening in the cliff, a cave he had never noticed, hidden in shadow. Faint gold light spilling, reflecting in a tiny pool below the entrance.

An idea: far less neat, far less precise, much more practical. “Could I borrow your pouch, and perhaps a length of sturdy rope? The kind that doesn’t mind a tug?”

Basil, obliging, delighted to share, provided them with a flourish. Instead of sprinkling, Pudding tied the pouch to a long thick vine, deep forest green, and attached it to Button’s tiny harness—knitted himself, for safety and comfort. “Now, Button. You are light. You are quick. You can fly, just a little, along the vine, and nudge the pouch towards the broken parts. I will steady you.”

Button clucked determinedly, quivering with readiness. She nudged the pouch with her beak, fluttering just enough, Pudding lowering her along the vine, a tiny brave aviator. Dust rained, not perfectly, not in neat piles, strategically enough to hold the bridge with a soft glowing mend. Teamwork.

Pip, from the far side, clapped so hard her wings blurred. “A diagram of that, please!” Pudding did not draw one. The mend was slightly lumpy. It held.

They stepped onto the reinforced bridge, Button’s claws finding purchase on the slightly uneven, magically strong surface. At the Sunken Spire they gathered Moonpetal Cloud-Berries, scent like sweet moonlight made tangible. Pudding picked only what the festival needed and left the rest for the mountain. Button ate one seed by accident and looked briefly cosmic, then merely hen again.

On the way back Pudding paused at the cave. The gold was not treasure: a vein of phosphorescent moss, beautiful, harmless, ethereal glow. He did not take it. He did look, which felt like enough.

The Flutterwings were ecstatic. “Magnificent!” Pip flitted around his head. “Bravery, strength! Such a clever plan to mend the bridge! So inventive!”

Pudding’s slow gentle smile crinkled his eyes. He had not been brave in their sense. Careful. Observant. Reliant on his friend.

Basil tucked the empty pouch away, already inventing a sequel charm that would, Pudding suspected, require even tinier sprinkling. “Do call if the vine ever needs a footnote.”

Sun dipped, peach and violet. By the window, a single Moonpetal Cloud-Berry on a saucer, faint glow against twilight. “A good day, Button. Not too much fuss. No one is likely to volunteer me for anything exciting for at least a week. Perhaps two.”

Button nudged his finger, a contented cluck. No grand pronouncements. Trust. The second biscuit, when it came, tasted as if it had been waiting politely the whole time.
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing distant-lands fantasy for independent readers
